name: Local and Air-Gapped Model Deployment
title: Local and Air-Gapped Model Deployment
answer: Local and air-gapped model deployment means running an AI model on hardware the firm or legal department controls, rather than sending data to a vendor's cloud API. In an air-gapped setup, that hardware has no connection to the public internet, so prompts, documents and outputs never leave the controlled environment. For legal operations this covers matter files, privileged communications, client confidential data, contract analysis, e-discovery review and internal knowledge search. The scope also includes the policies, access controls and audit trails that make such a deployment defensible. It is distinct from using a hosted model with a data processing agreement, because the security boundary is physical and network-based rather than contractual.

sections.body: Local and air-gapped model deployment means running an AI model on hardware the firm or legal department controls, rather than sending data to a vendor's cloud API. In an air-gapped setup, that hardware has no connection to the public internet, so prompts, documents and outputs never leave the controlled environment. For legal operations this covers matter files, privileged communications, client confidential data, contract analysis, e-discovery review and internal knowledge search. The scope also includes the policies, access controls and audit trails that make such a deployment defensible. It is distinct from using a hosted model with a data processing agreement, because the security boundary is physical and network-based rather than contractual.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The hardware is typically a rack server or workstation with one or more GPUs, sometimes a secure enclave or a dedicated appliance, plus local storage for model weights and vector indexes. The software stack includes an inference server such as llama.cpp, vLLM or Ollama, a local vector database for retrieval, and a thin internal API that legal applications call. Models are usually open-weight families that can be downloaded once and then moved across the air gap on encrypted removable media. Network isolation is enforced by firewall rules, disabled wireless interfaces and physical controls on ports and consoles. Power, cooling and physical access to the room are part of the infrastructure too.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A team selects a model that fits the task and the hardware, verifies its checksum and license, then converts or quantizes it to run efficiently on the available GPUs. The model is loaded into the inference server, and legal applications reach it through a local endpoint that mimics a cloud API, so existing prompts and workflows can be reused. For document-heavy work, a retrieval layer indexes the firm's own files and passes relevant passages to the model at query time. Evaluation is done with a held-out set of legal tasks, and outputs are logged for review. Updates arrive as new model files and are tested in a staging environment before they cross into production.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The first question is the license attached to the model weights, because some open-weight releases permit commercial use and others do not, and the provenance of training data can affect copyright exposure. This site tracks 148 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, which shows why firms document where a model came from and what data it was trained on. Privilege and confidentiality depend on keeping the air gap intact, so access logs, role-based controls and retention rules must be auditable. Compliance teams also map the deployment against the 6979 state AI bills tracked here, since local hosting does not exempt a firm from disclosure or bias rules. A model card, a data flow diagram and a signed internal policy are common artifacts in a defensible program.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Smaller and more capable open-weight models are making local deployment practical on a single workstation, not just a server room. Quantization and distillation are reducing the hardware needed, while confidential computing and hardware security modules aim to protect models and data even from the host operating system. Legal operations teams are likely to see hybrid patterns, where sensitive matters stay air-gapped and less sensitive work uses a controlled cloud. Regulators are adding pressure in the other direction, with state bills and court rules that may require disclosure of AI use, which local logging can support. The direction is toward more capable local models, tighter integration with document management systems, and clearer provenance records for every model that enters the air gap.
